newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania debt sound now, faces post-election test.
newsitem.headline: Romania debt sound now, faces post-election test.

text.p: Mounting economic woes should not scare investors from Romania's external debt for now but November election results will bring a real credibility test, central bank chief economist Daniel Daianu said on Friday.
Daianu discounted market rumours that Romania might suffer a cut in its credit rating only months after returning to capital markets after a decade-long absence.
"I think a downgrade now would be an over-reaction," Daianu told Reuters. "If the elections were two years away then I would be worried but the ballot is in two months time."

Romania's leftist government has been strongly criticised for short-term pre-election moves to keep the local leu currency high and inflation down. Exports fell as they borrowed heavily, subsidised industry and farming and delayed reform.

"The election is creating a pre-requisite for a change of policy in the right direction," said Daianu. "The new government needs to take tough measures. In my personal view we need a new macro-economic stabilisation package."
He said he was confident Romania would be successful in its short-term borrowing programme, which includes a $175 million syndicated loan due to close on September 16.
Romania launched its first Eurobonds and Samurais this year, raising around $750 million.
Daianu refused to speculate on the degree of political will that might exist, in what is expected to be some sort of centrist coalition government, to implement painful reforms.

But without a depreciation of the leu, higher interest rates, wage and cost restraints, budget deficit controls and reforms to attract substantial investment Romania will face a troubled future as debt servicing costs rocket, he said.

Monetary policy changes would need to be swift to be effective and to create the climate for investors who have so far shied from Romania, wary of legal snares, slow privatisation and an uncertain political climate.
"I think many people realise the need for a dramatic policy change. We have a choice to make," said Daianu, calling for a new government to build a consistent economic strategy.

His words reflect disappoint amongst reformist circles in Romania that six years after communism the country lags well behind its neighbours in attracting investment and setting up free-market institutions and legal protocols.
"We badly need foreign capital. We would be naive to assume that we can restructure this economy by ourselves."

Romania is the only former communist state not to have had an opposition government and its critics say its institutions are still run by ex-party functionaries suspicious of capitalism who are working to feather their own nests.

Its industries are still largely state-run and famously inefficient. Unemployment is at a statistically suspicious low and President Ion Iliescu, expected to retain his post in November, has advocated cautious reform that protects jobs.

Daianu said he countered his fear reforms will be delayed with the hope that a growing grey economy of small businesses and the irreversibility of privatisation would create a profit-orientated environment, whatever party was in power.

"Export-led growth is the only way to a healthy economy," he added. "We need a steady upgrade of the manufacturing base and an agrarian policy because our countryside is a potential gold mine for which there is no strategy."
